questions.questionMd: According to SMART notation, which formula defines the logarithmic TF variant (symbol `l`) for a term with a non-zero count?

options.text: `1 + log(tf)`
`tf / (1 + log(tf))`
`log(tf) - 1`

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, the logarithmic TF variant `l` is defined as `1 + log(tf)` for non-zero term frequency.

questions.questionMd: The Soundex algorithm is best described as a tool designed for which specific purpose?

options.text: Ranking spelling correction candidates by their edit distance from a misspelled query
General-purpose spelling correction for any English vocabulary term
Phonetic matching of proper names by encoding names that sound similar to the same code
Wildcard query resolution by hashing vocabulary terms into fixed-length codes

questions.explanationMd: Soundex is a phonetic coding algorithm, mainly useful for matching names that sound alike even when spelled differently.

questions.questionMd: An Elasticsearch deployment uses the `english` language analyzer. Based on the lecture content, which stemming algorithm does this analyzer apply by default?

options.text: Porter stemming
Lancaster stemming
Snowball multilingual stemming
WordNet lemmatization

questions.explanationMd: The lecture notes identify Porter stemming as the default stemming behavior for the English analyzer.

questions.questionMd: Why does the phrase query `"machine learning"` return fewer results than the Boolean query `machine AND learning`?

options.text: The phrase query automatically removes stop words, reducing the candidate set before merging
The phrase query restricts matching to document titles, whereas the Boolean AND searches the full text
The phrase query additionally requires the two terms to appear consecutively in the correct order
The phrase query applies a Jaccard similarity threshold that the Boolean AND does not use

questions.explanationMd: A phrase query requires adjacency and order, while a Boolean AND only requires both terms to occur somewhere in the document.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly represents the order of the seven stages in the standard IR pipeline introduced in Week 1?

options.text: Crawl → Index → Preprocess → Query Processing → Evaluate → Rank → Present
Query Processing → Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Rank → Evaluate → Present
Preprocess → Crawl → Index → Rank → Query Processing → Present → Evaluate
Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Query Processing → Rank → Present → Evaluate

questions.explanationMd: The pipeline first collects documents, preprocesses them, builds the index, then handles queries, ranks, presents, and evaluates results.

questions.questionMd: According to the length normalization worked example in the lecture notes, when two documents contain a query term the same number of times but differ in length, how does BM25 treat the shorter document?

options.text: The shorter document receives a higher TF saturation score because its length is below average, signalling greater topical focus
The shorter document receives a lower TF saturation score because BM25 penalizes documents with few total tokens
The shorter document is excluded from ranking because BM25 requires a minimum document length relative to `avgdl`
Both documents receive identical TF saturation scores because BM25 only compares document length to `k1`, not to `avgdl`

questions.explanationMd: BM25 normalizes by document length; for the same term count, a shorter-than-average document receives a stronger term-frequency signal.

questions.questionMd: After L2 normalization is applied to all document vectors in the Vector Space Model, what geometric property do all normalized document vectors share?

options.text: All normalized document vectors lie on the unit sphere, meaning their Euclidean norm equals 1
All normalized document vectors have the same direction as the query vector for the collection's most common query
All normalized document vectors become orthogonal to one another, eliminating redundant documents
All normalized document vectors are projected onto a two-dimensional plane to enable fast ranking

questions.explanationMd: L2 normalization scales every vector so its Euclidean length is 1, placing it on the unit sphere.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, a biword index stores every consecutive pair of terms as a single index entry. What is the primary drawback of this approach compared to a positional index?

options.text: Vocabulary size grows quadratically, from `N` terms to potentially `N²` bigrams, and it cannot support arbitrary phrase lengths
It requires storing token positions for every document, making it 2–4 times larger than a basic inverted index
It is slower to build than a positional index because every bigram must be stemmed separately
It cannot be combined with stopword removal because bigrams containing stopwords must be retained

questions.explanationMd: Biword indexes can explode the dictionary size and only handle phrase constraints through adjacent pairs, not arbitrary phrase lengths cleanly.

questions.questionMd: The two-pointer AND merge achieves `O(m + n)` time complexity only because of one crucial property of postings lists. What is that property?

options.text: Postings lists contain positional information for each document
Postings lists are stored in sorted order of document ID
Postings lists are stored in order of decreasing term frequency
Postings lists use variable-byte encoded gaps between document IDs

questions.explanationMd: The two-pointer merge works linearly because both lists are sorted by document ID.

questions.questionMd: R-Precision is defined as Precision computed at rank `R`, where `R` is which quantity?

options.text: The value of the fixed cutoff `k` chosen by the evaluator
The total number of relevant documents for that query in the collection
The rank of the first relevant document returned by the system
The ratio of retrieved documents to total collection size

questions.explanationMd: R-Precision evaluates precision at the cutoff equal to the number of relevant documents for that query.

questions.questionMd: A developer wants to build a faceted navigation sidebar that counts how many products belong to each category, such as `Electronics: 120` and `Clothing: 85`. Which field type should the category field use in the OpenSearch mapping?

options.text: `integer`, because aggregation requires numeric fields to produce accurate bucket counts
`text` with the `english` analyzer, so that category names are stemmed before aggregation
`text`, because it supports full-text analysis which enables partial matching of category names
`keyword`, because it stores exact unanalyzed values that can be used in terms aggregations

questions.explanationMd: Facet counts require exact bucket values, so `keyword` is the correct field type for terms aggregations.

questions.questionMd: PubMed, arXiv, and GitHub Code Search are all examples of which category of IR system?

options.text: Vertical search — domain-specific retrieval over a specialised corpus
Enterprise search — internal document retrieval within an organisation
Conversational IR — answer synthesis rather than ranked document retrieval
Multimedia IR — retrieval using images or audio as the query

questions.explanationMd: These systems search specialized domains rather than the entire web, so they are vertical search systems.

questions.questionMd: In Apache Lucene's segment-based architecture, what happens when a document is updated?

options.text: The existing segment is opened and the document's fields are overwritten in place
The document is moved to a special update buffer that replaces the original segment during the next merge
The old document is marked as deleted and the updated version is written as a new entry
All segments containing that document are merged immediately to apply the update atomically

questions.explanationMd: Lucene segments are immutable; updates are implemented as delete-plus-add operations.

questions.questionMd: When the two postings lists being merged with skip pointers have approximately equal lengths, what effect do skip pointers have on performance?

options.text: The merge terminates earlier than the naive case because both lists can skip simultaneously
Skip pointers have no effect at all because they are only stored for lists longer than 10,000 entries
Skip pointers provide the largest speedup because both lists benefit equally from jumping ahead
The overhead of checking skip conditions at each step can make performance marginally worse than the naive merge

questions.explanationMd: Skip checks add overhead, and equal-length lists often provide fewer useful opportunities to jump ahead.

questions.questionMd: Which statement best captures the concept of TF saturation as modelled by BM25 and log-TF?

options.text: Each additional occurrence of a term contributes equally to the relevance score regardless of how many times it has already appeared
TF saturation increases the weight of the first occurrence of a term and sets all subsequent occurrences to zero
Each additional occurrence of a term contributes progressively less to the relevance score
TF saturation means that once a term appears more than `k1` times, it is completely ignored in scoring

questions.explanationMd: TF saturation models diminishing returns: repeated term occurrences still help, but each new occurrence helps less.

questions.questionMd: Using the DCG formula `rel_i / log₂(i + 1)`, what is the position discount factor applied to a document at rank 2?

options.text: Exactly 1.00, because rank 2 is still in the top results and receives no discount
Exactly 0.50, because rank 2 halves the contribution relative to rank 1
Approximately 0.63, because `log₂(3) ≈ 1.585` and `1/1.585 ≈ 0.63`
Approximately 0.43, because `log₂(5) ≈ 2.322` and `1/2.322 ≈ 0.43`

questions.explanationMd: At rank 2, the discount denominator is `log₂(2+1)=log₂(3)≈1.585`, so the factor is about `0.63`.

questions.questionMd: Which 1960s development is credited as the first systematic, reproducible evaluation of IR systems, establishing the methodology of using test collections and relevance judgments?

options.text: The launch of MEDLARS at the National Library of Medicine
The SMART system developed by Salton at Cornell
The Cranfield experiments
The introduction of Luhn's automatic keyword extraction

questions.explanationMd: The Cranfield experiments established the reusable test collection methodology for IR evaluation.

questions.questionMd: Why is cosine similarity preferred over the raw dot product for ranking documents in the Vector Space Model?

options.text: Cosine similarity produces scores in the range [-1, 1] while dot products are unbounded
Cosine similarity normalizes for document length, preventing longer documents from automatically scoring higher than shorter, more focused ones
Cosine similarity is faster to compute than the dot product for large sparse vectors
Cosine similarity accounts for term order, while the dot product does not

questions.explanationMd: Cosine similarity compares vector direction after length normalization, reducing the bias toward long documents.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, the scheme `lnc.ltc` specifies which combination of weighting choices for documents and queries respectively?

options.text: Documents use log-TF, no IDF, no normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use log-TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use natural TF, cosine normalization, no IDF; queries use log-TF, IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: `lnc` means log TF, no IDF, cosine normalization for documents; `ltc` means log TF, IDF, cosine normalization for queries.

questions.questionMd: A term is best defined as which of the following in the context of information retrieval indexing?

options.text: Any single occurrence of a word anywhere in a document collection
A token produced by splitting raw text on whitespace boundaries
A normalized type that survives all preprocessing steps and enters the inverted index
A unique word form in the vocabulary before any normalization is applied

questions.explanationMd: A term is the normalized form that actually becomes an index entry.

questions.questionMd: As the raw term frequency `tf` in a document increases toward infinity, what value does the BM25 TF saturation function `tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1)` approach?

options.text: The value `k1 + 1`, which is the asymptotic maximum that the saturation function never exceeds
The value `tf`, meaning the saturation function converges back to raw TF at very high counts
The value 1, because the saturation function is normalized to the range [0, 1]
The value `k1`, which acts as a hard ceiling on TF contributions

questions.explanationMd: As `tf` becomes very large, the highest-order terms dominate and the fraction tends to `k1 + 1`.

questions.questionMd: In a standard TREC qrels file, each line maps a `(query_id, doc_id)` pair to a relevance label. What does a grade of 0 in a graded qrels file signify?

options.text: The document is partially relevant — useful but not a complete answer
The document was not in the judgment pool and was therefore never assessed
The query was retired and no longer active in the evaluation campaign
The document was judged by a human assessor and found to be irrelevant to the query

questions.explanationMd: A qrels grade of 0 means the document was assessed and judged non-relevant.

questions.questionMd: What is the effect of setting the BM25 parameter `k1` to a very large value, approaching infinity?

options.text: TF saturation disappears and the scoring approaches raw TF with no diminishing returns
The BM25 score becomes equivalent to a binary Boolean match signal
Length normalization is disabled and all documents are treated as having equal length
The IDF component is scaled down and rare terms receive lower weights

questions.explanationMd: Large `k1` weakens saturation, so term frequency behaves more like raw TF.

questions.questionMd: When constructing an 11-point interpolated Precision-Recall curve, how is interpolated Precision defined at a given recall level `r`?

options.text: The arithmetic mean of Precision values immediately before and after recall level `r`
The Precision value recorded the first time recall `r` is reached during retrieval
The minimum Precision across all recall levels `r′ > r`, to represent a pessimistic bound
The maximum Precision achieved at any recall level `r′` that is greater than or equal to `r`

questions.explanationMd: Interpolated precision uses the best precision observed at any recall level at or above the target recall.

questions.questionMd: Expanding a search to retrieve more candidate documents generally increases recall. What is the typical effect on precision?

options.text: Precision tends to decrease because more irrelevant documents enter the result set
Precision and recall always move in the same direction under any retrieval strategy
Precision increases proportionally because a larger result set exposes more relevant documents
Precision is unaffected because it is computed over only the relevant documents retrieved

questions.explanationMd: Broadening retrieval often captures more relevant documents but also introduces more non-relevant ones, reducing precision.

questions.questionMd: A spelling corrector using a Jaccard threshold of 0.2 consistently returns no candidates for misspelled words of four characters or fewer. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Edit distance computation fails on short strings because the dynamic programming table is too small
Short words are automatically classified as stop words and excluded from the k-gram index
The k-gram index only indexes vocabulary terms of five characters or more by default
Short words produce very few k-grams, so Jaccard scores are inherently lower

questions.explanationMd: Short strings generate very few k-grams, so even small differences can produce low Jaccard overlap.

questions.questionMd: The NLTK English stopword list contains approximately how many words, and what is the approximate size of Lucene's default stopword list?

options.text: 179 words in NLTK and approximately 33 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene
500 words in NLTK and approximately 100 in Lucene
33 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene

questions.explanationMd: The lecture notes state that NLTK has about 179 English stopwords, while Lucene's default English stop set is much smaller, about 33 words.

questions.questionMd: In a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) computation, a query returns a ranked list in which no relevant document appears anywhere in the results. What Reciprocal Rank value is assigned to this query?

options.text: 0.0, because no relevant document was found
The query is excluded from the MRR calculation to avoid distorting the mean
0.5, as the midpoint value for a partial retrieval failure
1.0, because the metric defaults to the maximum when the query cannot be penalised further

questions.explanationMd: If there is no relevant result, the reciprocal rank is defined as 0.

questions.questionMd: A corpus contains 1000 documents, and the term `quasar` appears in exactly 50 of them. Applying the formula `IDF(t) = log(N / df(t))`, what is the IDF of `quasar`?
questions.explanationMd: `N/df = 1000/50 = 20`, so the IDF is `log(20)`, approximately 3.0 with natural log.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, which traversal strategy is the standard approach in modern IR systems for accumulating TF-IDF scores?

options.text: TAAT (Term At A Time), which processes one term across all matching documents before moving to the next
DAAT (Document At A Time), which processes all terms in a document simultaneously before moving to the next document
TAAT (Term At A Time), which is faster because it avoids the need for a score accumulator
DAAT (Document At A Time), which processes one document at a time and accumulates scores in a dictionary

questions.explanationMd: The uploaded midterm marks the DAAT-style traversal as the expected lecture answer for modern score accumulation.

questions.questionMd: Why does the smoothed IDF formula `log(N / (df + 1)) + 1` add 1 to the denominator?

options.text: To ensure that every term receives an IDF value greater than 1 regardless of collection size
To bring the IDF range into alignment with the range produced by log-TF
To make very common terms receive a higher IDF than they would under the standard formula
To prevent division by zero when a term has never appeared in any document in the collection

questions.explanationMd: Adding 1 to `df` prevents division by zero for unseen terms.

questions.questionMd: How does a biword index handle a three-word phrase query such as `"machine learning model"`?

options.text: It falls back to a standard Boolean AND query over the three individual terms
It stores the entire three-word phrase as a single compound dictionary entry
It uses the positional index for any phrase longer than two words
It decomposes the phrase into overlapping biwords and executes an AND query over `machine_learning` and `learning_model`

questions.explanationMd: A biword index turns longer phrases into overlapping adjacent pairs and intersects the corresponding postings lists.

questions.questionMd: Which formula does BM25 use for the IDF component of a term `t` in a collection of `N` documents with document frequency `df(t)`?

options.text: `log(N / df(t))`

questions.explanationMd: BM25 commonly uses the Robertson-Sparck Jones style IDF with `+0.5` smoothing and an outer `+1` inside the log.

questions.questionMd: A system achieves `NDCG@k = 1.0` for a given query. What must be true?

options.text: `NDCG@k = 1.0` is impossible; values are strictly bounded below 1.0 in practice
The system's `DCG@k` equals zero, meaning no relevant documents were returned
The system retrieved exactly `k` documents, all of which are relevant
The system's ranking is identical to the ideal ranking

questions.explanationMd: NDCG is `DCG/IDCG`; a score of 1.0 means the ranking matches the ideal ordering at the cutoff.

questions.questionMd: Given two sorted postings lists of lengths `m` and `n`, what is the time complexity of the two-pointer AND merge algorithm?

options.text: `O(n²)`
`O(m log n)`

questions.explanationMd: Each pointer only moves forward through its list, so the total work is linear in the two list lengths.

questions.questionMd:
Given the ranked list `(R = relevant, I = irrelevant)` below, what is the Average Precision (AP)?

`R, I, I, R, R`
questions.explanationMd: Relevant documents occur at ranks 1, 4, and 5. AP = `(P@1 + P@4 + P@5) / 3 = (1 + 0.5 + 0.6) / 3 = 0.700`.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of the Boolean retrieval model?

options.text: Query processing time scales quadratically with the number of query terms
Results cannot be cached because they change with each query
The model cannot support the NOT operator on large corpora
A document that satisfies all but one query term is excluded entirely from results

questions.explanationMd: Strict Boolean matching has no partial credit or ranking; a near-match can be excluded completely.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, the NLTK WordNetLemmatizer called on the word `ran` without providing a POS tag will produce which incorrect output?

options.text: `runn`, because it applies a heuristic suffix-stripping rule
`ran` unchanged, because it defaults to treating the word as a noun
`go`, because it links irregular verb forms through WordNet
`run`, because it correctly identifies the past tense

questions.explanationMd: Without a POS tag, WordNetLemmatizer defaults to noun behavior and leaves `ran` unchanged.

questions.questionMd: Why is Normalized DCG (NDCG) preferred over raw DCG when comparing results across multiple queries?

options.text: Raw DCG rewards retrieving more documents, while NDCG penalizes systems that return more than `k` results
NDCG uses binary relevance labels, which are easier to collect than the graded labels required by raw DCG
NDCG applies a stricter position discount than DCG, making it more sensitive to early retrieval errors
NDCG normalizes by the ideal DCG so all queries map to [0, 1]

questions.explanationMd: Dividing by IDCG makes scores comparable across queries with different relevance distributions.

questions.questionMd: What is the typical relationship between Precision and Recall as more documents are retrieved?

options.text: Both Precision and Recall increase together as more documents are retrieved
Precision stays constant while Recall increases
Precision tends to decrease as Recall increases, reflecting a fundamental tradeoff
Recall decreases as Precision increases, because early ranks contain the best results

questions.explanationMd: Retrieving deeper increases the chance of finding more relevant documents but usually adds more irrelevant ones too.

questions.questionMd: In TREC-style evaluation, the pooling method is used to reduce annotation cost. What known bias does this approach introduce?

options.text: Documents in the pool receive inflated relevance scores because annotators see too many results at once
Pooling forces all systems to retrieve the same top-k documents, reducing result diversity
Documents outside the pool are treated as irrelevant
Annotators judge documents from all queries simultaneously, leading to topic confusion

questions.explanationMd: Unjudged documents outside the pool are commonly treated as non-relevant during evaluation, which can penalize systems finding novel relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: In an OpenSearch bool query, which clause excludes matching documents from the result set without contributing to the relevance score of remaining documents?

options.text: `must` with a negated term
`should` with `minimum_should_match` set to 0
`must_not`
`filter`

questions.explanationMd: `must_not` removes matching documents and runs in filter context, so it does not add to scores.

questions.questionMd: A user searches `automobile fuel efficiency`, but the most relevant document uses only the phrases `car gas mileage` and `vehicle consumption`. What problem does this scenario illustrate?

options.text: The precision-recall tradeoff — retrieving more documents lowers average result quality
The corpus freshness problem — the index has not been updated to include recent terminology
The stopword problem — common function words are masking the discriminating content terms
The vocabulary mismatch problem — lexical overlap is zero despite near-identical meaning

questions.explanationMd: The query and document use different words for the same meaning, which is the vocabulary mismatch problem.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a known limitation of the probabilistic IDF formula `log((N - df) / df)` as noted in the lecture?

options.text: The formula always returns the same value regardless of the collection size `N`
The formula cannot be computed when the document frequency is greater than 1
The formula doubles the IDF value of any term whose document frequency exceeds `N/2`
The formula can produce negative values, requiring careful handling in implementations

questions.explanationMd: When `df > N/2`, `(N-df)/df` is less than 1 and its log becomes negative.

questions.questionMd:
Using the inverted index for the three documents below, which document is returned by the Boolean AND query `cat AND sat`?

Doc 0: `the cat sat on the mat`

Doc 1: `the cat ate the rat`

Doc 2: `the rat sat and ate`

options.text: Doc 0 and Doc 2
Doc 0 only
Doc 0 and Doc 1
Doc 1 and Doc 2

questions.explanationMd: Only Doc 0 contains both `cat` and `sat`.

questions.questionMd: Variable-byte (VB) encoding uses a continuation bit within each byte. What does a continuation bit value of 1, the top bit set, indicate in VB encoding?

options.text: This is the last terminal byte of the current encoded number
This byte encodes a negative gap and should be subtracted
This byte is a continuation byte and more bytes follow for the current number
This byte marks the boundary between two separate encoded numbers

questions.explanationMd: In the lecture's VB convention, the high bit set to 1 marks the terminal byte of the encoded integer.

questions.questionMd: For a single query, the first relevant document appears at rank 3 in the result list. What is the Reciprocal Rank (RR) for this query?
What simplifying assumption does the Binary Independence Model (BIM) make about query terms when estimating the probability that a document is relevant?

options.text: Terms are assumed to be statistically independent of one another given the relevance status of the document
Terms are assumed to have equal document frequency across the entire collection
Terms are assumed to appear the same number of times in every relevant document in the collection
Terms are assumed to be ranked by their IDF value before any probability estimation is performed

questions.explanationMd: BIM assumes conditional independence of terms given relevance or non-relevance.

questions.questionMd: During a two-pointer AND merge, when the values at both pointers are equal, which pointers should be advanced?

options.text: The pointer into the list with the larger next value
Only the pointer into the first list
Both pointers must be advanced
Only the pointer into the shorter list

questions.explanationMd: When both doc IDs match, the document is emitted and both lists advance past it.

questions.questionMd: A researcher reports `p < 0.05` on a Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing two IR systems. A colleague argues this alone is insufficient to conclude that one system is better. Why is the colleague correct?

options.text: Statistical significance only rules out chance
The Wilcoxon test only applies to normally distributed data; using it on MAP scores is methodologically invalid
`p < 0.05` confirms the null hypothesis, meaning the systems perform identically on the query set
A Wilcoxon test requires at least 100 queries before p-values become meaningful, regardless of the result

questions.explanationMd: A p-value indicates evidence against chance variation, but practical importance and effect size still matter.

questions.questionMd: A basic inverted index returns documents containing both `space` and `shuttle` using an AND operation, but includes a document where these words appear far apart and in a different order. What type of index is needed to eliminate such false positives?

options.text: A biword index that stores every adjacent pair of terms as a single entry
A term-frequency index that weights terms by how often they co-occur
A positional index that stores token positions within each document
A compressed index that uses gap encoding to reduce postings list size

questions.explanationMd: A positional index allows the system to verify term order and distance inside each document.

questions.questionMd: Given two k-gram sets `A` and `B`, which expression correctly computes their Jaccard similarity?
questions.explanationMd: Jaccard similarity is intersection size divided by union size.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, in which of the following systems has BM25 been the default scorer?

options.text: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch since version 5.0, and Lucene since version 6.0
The Google PageRank algorithm as its primary term-matching component since 2010
Apache Spark MLlib and scikit-learn since their initial releases
The TREC evaluation framework as the only permitted baseline for ad-hoc retrieval tracks

questions.explanationMd: The lecture states that Lucene-based search engines use BM25 as the default scorer in those versions.

questions.questionMd: A search application requires that Recall be weighted more heavily than Precision. Which setting of `β` in the `Fβ` formula achieves this?

options.text: `β = 0`, because this setting removes Precision from the calculation entirely
`β = 1`, because this balances Precision and Recall and therefore emphasises neither
`β > 1`, because larger β values increase the weight assigned to Recall in the harmonic mean
`β < 1`, because smaller β values shift focus away from Precision toward Recall

questions.explanationMd: In `Fβ`, values of `β` greater than 1 emphasize recall more than precision.

questions.questionMd: During an AND merge with skip pointers, under what condition should the pointer in list `P₁` jump to the skip target rather than stepping forward by one?

options.text: When the skip target is within `⌊√p⌋` positions of the current index in `P₁`
When the value at the skip target position in `P₁` is strictly less than the current value in `P₂`
When the value at the skip target position in `P₁` is less than or equal to the current value in `P₂`
When the current value in `P₁` is greater than the current value in `P₂`

questions.explanationMd: The skip is safe when the skip target does not pass beyond the current comparison value in the other list.

questions.questionMd: Document A has 1000 tokens and mentions `space` 10 times. Document B has 100 tokens and mentions `space` 5 times. Which claim about TF-IDF scoring is correct?

options.text: Document B scores higher because its relative term frequency (5%) exceeds Document A's (1%)
Document A scores higher because a larger document contains more contextual evidence
Both documents receive identical TF-IDF scores because IDF is the same for both
Document A scores higher because raw term count always dominates TF-IDF computation

questions.explanationMd: With normalized TF, Document B has a higher relative frequency for the term.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `"fields": ["title^3", "body^1"]` inside a `multi_match` clause. What does the `^3` notation mean for the `title` field?

options.text: The query requires at least three matching terms in the `title` field before the document is considered a candidate
OpenSearch searches the `title` field three times before falling back to the `body` field
The `title` field is indexed three times to increase recall for title matches
A match in the `title` field contributes three times more to the relevance score than an equivalent match in the `body` field

questions.explanationMd: The `^3` syntax boosts matches in the `title` field by a factor of three.

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly describes a known limitation of offline IR evaluation using test collections?

options.text: Offline NDCG scores are always higher than online CTR metrics because they are computed over larger document sets
Test collections used in offline evaluation automatically update their qrels as new systems are submitted
Offline evaluation requires live user traffic and is therefore more expensive than online A/B testing
Gains in offline metrics do not always correspond to improvements in online user behavior metrics

questions.explanationMd: Offline metrics are proxies; improvements in them do not always translate to better user behavior in live systems.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, where do the document frequency (`df`) values required for both TF-IDF and BM25 computation come from at retrieval time?

options.text: From a separate per-document frequency table computed fresh at query time by scanning the corpus
From the average document length statistic `avgdl` stored alongside the inverted index
From the query itself, by counting how many query terms appear in a predefined stopword list
From the inverted index constructed during indexing, specifically from the length of each term's postings list

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency is the number of documents in a term's postings list, which is available from the inverted index.

questions.questionMd: What must a developer do in code when computing `NDCG@k` for a query that has no relevant documents in the collection?

options.text: Assign each retrieved document a relevance grade of 1 and recompute normally
Return 0.0 as a special-case guard, because `IDCG = 0` makes the formula undefined
Exclude that query from the evaluation and reduce `Q` by 1 in the MAP formula
Return 1.0, because a system cannot be penalised for a query with no correct answers

questions.explanationMd: If there are no relevant documents, `IDCG` is zero and `DCG/IDCG` is undefined, so code needs a guard value.

questions.questionMd: A corpus has `N = 100,000` tokens. Using Heap's Law with `k = 44` and `β = 0.49`, what is the approximate predicted vocabulary size?

options.text: Approximately 44,000 unique terms
Approximately 4,400 unique terms
Approximately 13,600 unique terms
Approximately 100,000 unique terms

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law gives `V = kN^β`; `44 * 100000^0.49` is roughly 13,600.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's compression data, combining gap encoding with VB encoding on a typical postings list achieves what overall compression factor compared to storing raw int32 doc_ids?

questions.questionMd: A developer uses `SELECT * FROM papers WHERE abstract LIKE '%heart attack%'` to find cardiology research. What is the most significant limitation of this approach compared to an IR system?

questions.questionMd: In the positional index approach to phrase queries, what is the role of the first phase?

It verifies that query terms appear at consecutive positions in each document

questions.questionMd: Using the standard IDF formula taught in lecture, how is `IDF(t)` computed for a term `t` given a collection of `N` documents where `t` appears in `df(t)` of them?

questions.questionMd: What is the key architectural difference between the BSBI and SPIMI index construction algorithms?

BSBI requires a global term-to-integer mapping across all blocks, while SPIMI does not
BSBI writes sorted postings directly to disk, while SPIMI keeps all postings in RAM permanently
BSBI is designed for single-pass processing, while SPIMI requires multiple passes over the corpus

questions.questionMd: A ranked list has graded relevance scores `[3, 1, 0, 2, 1]` at ranks 1 through 5. What is the approximate `DCG@5`?

3.000, because only the first rank contributes and its grade is 3
7.000, computed by summing the raw relevance grades `3+1+0+2+1`

questions.questionMd: Using VB encoding, a gap value of 5 requires how many bytes, and a gap value of 200 requires how many bytes?

1 byte for gap 5 and 1 byte for gap 200
2 bytes for gap 5 and 4 bytes for gap 200
1 byte for gap 5 and 2 bytes for gap 200

questions.questionMd: The log-average TF variant (symbol `L`) in SMART notation is defined as which of the following expressions?

`(1 + log tf) / (1 + log avg_tf(d))`

questions.questionMd: Why is leading a query with a NOT operator alone considered poor practice?

options.text: It can only be applied after an OR merge has been completed
It requires scanning the entire corpus to find all document IDs not in the negated list
It produces the same result as an AND query but takes longer to parse
It requires building a secondary inverted index from scratch at query time

questions.questionMd: In Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), relevance scores are divided by the log base-2 of `(rank + 1)`. What user behavior does this logarithmic discount model?

options.text: Users read results in random order, so position should have no effect on contribution
Users prefer documents that are only marginally relevant at high ranks over highly relevant documents at low ranks
User attention diminishes at lower ranks, so a relevant document at rank 10 is worth less than one at rank 1
The discount penalizes systems that retrieve more than `k` documents, keeping result sets short

questions.explanationMd: DCG models the idea that users pay more attention to early ranks than later ranks.

questions.questionMd: Heap's Law describes how vocabulary size `V` grows with the total number of tokens `N` in a corpus. Which statement correctly characterizes this growth?

options.text: Vocabulary growth stops once the corpus exceeds a threshold size
Vocabulary grows exponentially in proportion to the square of `N`
Vocabulary grows sub-linearly and never fully stops growing
Vocabulary grows linearly, adding a fixed number of new terms per document

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law predicts sublinear growth: new vocabulary appears more slowly over time, but growth does not completely stop.

questions.questionMd: Lucene uses a Finite State Transducer (FST) as its term dictionary structure. What property makes the FST particularly well-suited for this role?

It uses a B-tree structure to guarantee `O(log n)` insertion time when new terms are added to a mutable segment
It is a compact, memory-efficient graph that supports `O(len)` prefix and suffix lookups on the sorted term list
It stores postings lists in columnar format so that aggregations can be computed without loading all term data into RAM

questions.explanationMd: FSTs compactly encode sorted term dictionaries and support efficient lookup and prefix-style traversal.

questions.questionMd: What is the correct set of 3-grams with boundary markers for the vocabulary term `query`?

`qu$, que, uer, ery, ry$`
`$qu, que, uer, ery, ry$`

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, what does a query return?

options.text: A set of document IDs with no ordering or relevance scores
A probability distribution over matching documents
A ranked list of documents sorted by relevance score
A set of document IDs sorted by term frequency

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best explains why simple whitespace tokenization is insufficient for production search systems?

It always produces more tokens than a regex-based tokenizer would for the same input

questions.questionMd: In the IR triangle model, which concept sits at the centre connecting the query, the document, and the information need?

Precision
Vocabulary
Relevance

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly describes a key theoretical difference between BM25 and TF-IDF with cosine similarity?

TF-IDF is derived from the Probability Ranking Principle, while BM25 is an empirical approximation with no theoretical basis

Stopword removal can be skipped because rare terms never appear in large corpora
Compression is unnecessary because sub-linear growth keeps the index small
The entire index can be built in a single pass because vocabulary size is bounded

Sorting results by a numeric price field and computing aggregation buckets for faceted navigation
Storing the original human-readable content of a document so it can be displayed in search results
Finding all documents that contain the term `laptop` in a full-text search query

questions.explanationMd: DocValues are column-oriented field values used for sorting, aggregations, and similar operations.

A mapping
A segment
An index

questions.questionMd: A system retrieves 5 documents for a query that has 10 relevant documents, and all 5 retrieved documents are relevant and ranked perfectly. What is the maximum possible AP for this query?

0.75, because partial retrieval is penalised by a fixed 25% reduction in AP
0.0, because MAP requires all relevant documents to be retrieved before assigning any credit

questions.questionMd: What is the time complexity of BSBI expressed in terms of `T`, the total number of token occurrences in the corpus?

`O(T log N)` where `N` is the number of documents
`O(T log T)` due to the dominant sorting step
`O(T²)` because every token pair must be compared during the merge phase

questions.questionMd: Why does a term that appears in every document in a corpus receive an IDF score of zero?

Because the logarithm function is undefined when the document frequency equals zero
Because stopword removal deletes the term before the IDF calculation is performed
Because universal terms inflate TF scores and must be cancelled by a negative IDF

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch index is created with 3 primary shards. After the index goes into production, the team finds that data has grown and they need more shards. What is the correct approach?

Update the index settings at runtime to increase the number of primary shards
Increase the replica count, which automatically redistributes documents across more shards
Create a new index with the desired shard count and reindex all documents into it

questions.questionMd: Why do high-frequency terms with large document frequency achieve better compression ratios than rare terms when gap encoding combined with VB encoding is applied?

High-frequency terms have shorter string representations in the dictionary, reducing total index size
High-frequency terms benefit from front-coding in the dictionary, independently of the postings lists

questions.questionMd: A new retrieval system retrieves a highly relevant document that was not included in the TREC judgment pool. How does this affect the system's measured evaluation score?

The evaluation is restarted with an expanded pool that includes the new system's results
The document receives the highest relevance grade automatically, rewarding novel retrieval
The document is treated as irrelevant because it was never judged, which unfairly penalises the system

questions.questionMd: On a log-log plot of term rank vs. term frequency, what shape does Zipf's Law predict?

A concave curve that levels off as rank increases
A straight line with a positive slope
A straight line with a slope of approximately -1

questions.questionMd: What practical implication does Zipf's Law have for the design of a stopword list?

Zipf's Law predicts that stopword removal will have no measurable effect on vocabulary size
Zipf's Law implies that all terms above a fixed frequency threshold carry equal information

questions.questionMd: Compared to the original forward dictionary, approximately how much larger does the permuterm index grow?

Roughly 2 times larger

Documents are always evenly distributed across shards regardless of dataset size, eliminating hot-spot shards

questions.questionMd: What retrieval behavior results when the BM25 parameter `k1` is set to 0?

questions.questionMd: In the BSBI algorithm, after each RAM-sized block is processed and written to disk, what operation combines all on-disk blocks into the final inverted index?

An external k-way merge sort over all sorted block files
A second full pass over the original corpus to resolve term_id collisions
A binary search tree insertion that merges block entries one term at a time

questions.questionMd: Why does the Vector Space Model use cosine similarity rather than Euclidean distance to compare document and query vectors?

Euclidean distance cannot be computed for high-dimensional vectors, whereas cosine similarity is defined for any number of dimensions
Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than Euclidean distance for sparse TF-IDF vectors

BSBI requires a global term-to-integer dictionary to be maintained across all blocks
BSBI cannot handle corpora larger than available RAM because it performs no disk-based operations

questions.questionMd: Embedding skip pointers into a postings list at index build time introduces which tradeoff?

questions.questionMd: Mean Average Precision (MAP) penalizes a system that fails to retrieve some relevant documents. Why?

MAP is computed only over queries where the system retrieved at least one relevant document, excluding all others

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of Boolean retrieval that motivates the move to ranked retrieval?

questions.questionMd: After intersecting k-gram postings to resolve a wildcard query, why is a mandatory post-filtering step required?

options.text: [3, 11, 22, 45, 56] stored unchanged because the first value is already a gap

questions.explanationMd: Gap encoding stores the first docID and then differences: `3, 11-3=8, 22-11=11, 45-22=23, 56-45=11`.

questions.questionMd: A search application needs to find news articles about `space exploration` published after January 1, 2024, ranked by relevance. How should the date constraint be placed in the OpenSearch Query DSL to achieve the best performance?

options.text: In the `should` clause of a bool query, giving a score boost to articles published after the cutoff date
In the `must` clause of a bool query, so that it contributes positively to the relevance score for recent articles
In the `filter` clause of a bool query, because filter context is cached and does not affect the relevance score
As a top-level range query outside any bool wrapper, since date fields cannot be nested inside compound queries

questions.explanationMd: The date constraint is a non-scoring condition, so it belongs in filter context for caching and efficiency.

questions.questionMd: When optimizing a multi-term AND query by sorting operands in order of ascending document frequency, what is the primary benefit?

options.text: Intermediate result sets shrink fastest when processing begins with the rarest terms
The total number of postings lists loaded into memory is reduced
The OR merge step is eliminated from the query plan
Skip pointers become unnecessary for the remaining operations

questions.explanationMd: Intersecting rare terms first keeps intermediate postings results small.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly describes the three-stage spelling correction pipeline?

options.text: K-gram candidate retrieval → Jaccard similarity filtering → edit distance ranking
Edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval
Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking
K-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering

questions.explanationMd: The typical pipeline first retrieves candidates by k-grams, filters by Jaccard overlap, then ranks by edit distance.

questions.questionMd: In OpenSearch's two-phase query execution model, what does the coordinating node do during the fetch phase?

options.text: It writes the query result to a distributed cache so that repeated queries are served without contacting the shards again
It collects global term statistics from every shard before any scoring takes place
It selects the global top-k documents by merging shard scores, then retrieves from the relevant shards
It broadcasts the query to all shards and waits for each shard to score its local documents

questions.explanationMd: The coordinating node merges shard results to identify global top documents and fetches the required document data from the relevant shards.

questions.questionMd: Under the TREC standard four-point graded relevance scale, which grade label is assigned to a document that is a perfect, exact answer to the query?

options.text: 1 — Partially relevant
3 — Perfectly relevant
2 — Highly relevant
4 — Authoritative source

questions.explanationMd: The lecture scale uses grade 3 for a perfectly relevant document.

questions.questionMd: The sentence `The cat sat on the mat` contains how many tokens and how many types respectively?

options.text: 6 tokens and 5 types
5 tokens and 5 types
5 tokens and 6 types
6 tokens and 6 types

questions.explanationMd: There are six word occurrences, but `the` repeats, so there are five distinct types if case is normalized.

questions.questionMd: Recall measures which aspect of retrieval performance?

options.text: The average precision at each recall level across multiple queries
The rank position of the first relevant document in the result list
The fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant
The fraction of all relevant documents that were successfully retrieved

questions.explanationMd: Recall is relevant retrieved divided by all relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: In the Vector Space Model, why are document vectors described as sparse?

options.text: Vectors are sparse because cosine normalization sets most small weights to zero during L2 normalization
Most vocabulary terms do not appear in any given document
Document vectors are sparse because only the top-k highest-weighted terms are stored to save memory
Sparsity arises because IDF values are rounded to zero for any term with document frequency above a threshold

questions.explanationMd: A document contains only a small subset of the total vocabulary, so most vector dimensions are zero.

questions.questionMd: Crawling, text preprocessing, and index construction are all classified as offline pipeline stages. What is the primary architectural reason for this design choice?

options.text: Online stages require specialised hardware that cannot also execute indexing workloads
Offline stages consume too much RAM to run concurrently with live query traffic
Preprocessing must be performed after each user query to reflect the most recent document versions
Building the index in advance allows online query processing to complete within strict millisecond latency budgets

questions.explanationMd: Expensive collection and indexing work is done before query time so search can respond quickly.

questions.questionMd: Three terms are compared for VB compression efficiency: a high-frequency term appearing in 45 documents, a medium-frequency term in 15 documents, and a rare term in 3 documents. Which achieves the highest compression ratio and why?

options.text: The high-frequency term
The rare term, because fewer postings entries means less data to compress overall
All three achieve identical compression ratios because VB encoding is independent of term frequency
The medium-frequency term, because it balances gap size and postings list length optimally

questions.explanationMd: High-frequency terms usually have smaller docID gaps, so gap plus VB encoding compresses them more efficiently.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, which of the following statements about BM25 scores is correct?

options.text: BM25 scores are ordinal relevance estimates and should not be compared across different queries
BM25 scores are symmetric, meaning the score for query Q against document D equals the score for D against Q
BM25 scores are calibrated probabilities that sum to 1 across all documents for a given query
BM25 scores always fall within the range [0, 1] because the IDF component is bounded by `log(N)`

questions.explanationMd: BM25 scores rank documents for a query; they are not calibrated probabilities and should not be compared directly across queries.

questions.questionMd: When building a k-gram index for general English text information retrieval, which value of `k` is described as the recommended tradeoff between index size and retrieval precision?
questions.explanationMd: The lecture notes describe 3-grams as a common tradeoff between index size and candidate precision.

questions.questionMd: Which stemmer described in the lectures is characterized as the most aggressive, producing the smallest vocabulary but the highest over-stemming error rate?

options.text: Snowball
WordNet lemmatizer
Lancaster
Porter

questions.explanationMd: Lancaster stemming is known as more aggressive than Porter or Snowball.

questions.questionMd: When two sorted postings lists are merged with OR and both pointers point to the same document ID, what is the correct action?

options.text: Skip the document ID entirely because it indicates an AND match, not an OR match
Emit the document ID once and advance only the pointer into the shorter list
Emit the document ID twice to reflect it appears in both lists and advance both pointers
Emit the document ID once and advance both pointers

questions.explanationMd: In a set union, duplicates are emitted once, then both lists advance.

questions.questionMd: In the SMART notation table, the augmented TF variant (symbol `a`) is defined as which of the following?

options.text: `1 + log(tf / max_tf(d))`
`tf / (tf + max_tf(d))`
`0.5 * log(tf) + 0.5 * max_tf(d)`

questions.explanationMd: The augmented TF formula scales raw TF by the maximum term frequency in the document and maps it into `[0.5, 1]`.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which scenario represents a case where stopword removal should not be applied?

options.text: A phrase query such as `to be or not to be`
Preprocessing queries submitted to a web-scale search engine
Indexing a large corpus of general news articles
A keyword query for a common technical term like `network`

questions.explanationMd: For phrase queries, stopwords may be essential to the exact meaning and word sequence.

questions.questionMd: A rare term appears in only one shard of a 5-shard OpenSearch index. Without any correction, how does this affect BM25 scoring for that term?

options.text: The shard containing that term computes an artificially high IDF because its local document count is much smaller than the global total
The term is assigned a zero IDF score because the coordinating node cannot find it on all shards simultaneously
The term is excluded from scoring because OpenSearch requires a term to appear on at least two shards to be indexed
The term receives a lower-than-global IDF because each shard divides its local IDF by the total number of shards

questions.explanationMd: With local shard statistics, a rare term may receive an inflated IDF on the shard where it appears.

questions.questionMd: A colleague argues that MAP is always preferable to `NDCG@k` because MAP considers the entire ranked list rather than a cutoff. Which counter-argument best explains a key limitation of MAP?

options.text: MAP assumes binary relevance
MAP is only defined for navigational queries where exactly one relevant document exists
MAP penalises systems that retrieve more than `k` documents, making deep retrieval unfair
MAP requires a larger query set than `NDCG@k` to produce stable estimates

questions.explanationMd: MAP is based on binary relevance and cannot directly model graded usefulness like NDCG.

questions.questionMd: A standard IR test collection consists of exactly three required components. Which of the following correctly identifies all three?

options.text: A training set, a validation set, and a held-out test set
An inverted index, a stemmer, and a stop-word list
A fixed corpus, standardized topics, and human relevance judgments (qrels)
A ranked retrieval model, a query parser, and a relevance feedback module

questions.explanationMd: A classic IR test collection contains documents, topics/queries, and relevance judgments.

questions.questionMd: A term has a document frequency (DF) of 500 and a term frequency (TF) of 12 in one particular document. What does the DF value of 500 indicate?

options.text: The term appears 500 times across all documents combined
The term's postings list contains 500 position entries
The term appears in 500 different documents in the corpus
The term appears in documents with an average length of 500 tokens

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency counts how many distinct documents contain the term.

questions.questionMd: How does TF-IDF enable keyword extraction from a single document within a larger corpus?

options.text: Terms whose raw TF exceeds the collection average document frequency are selected as keywords regardless of their IDF value
Terms with the lowest TF-IDF weight are the best keywords because they are unique to the document and appear nowhere else
Terms with the highest TF-IDF weight in a document are strong candidate keywords for that document
Terms are selected as keywords when their IDF value equals zero, indicating they are universally recognized concepts

questions.explanationMd: High TF-IDF terms are frequent in the document but relatively distinctive in the collection, making them good keyword candidates.

questions.questionMd: In IR system design, Boolean retrieval and neural reranking sit at opposite ends of a fundamental tradeoff. Which pair of terms correctly names the two competing goals?

options.text: Precision (result quality) versus recall (result completeness)
Efficiency (speed and scale) versus effectiveness (accuracy and relevance)
Index compression versus index coverage
Offline processing versus online processing

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval emphasizes fast scalable matching; neural reranking often improves relevance at higher computational cost.

questions.questionMd: Which organisation established TREC (Text REtrieval Conference) in 1992 to provide shared benchmarks for IR evaluation?

options.text: DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)
IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
ACM (Association for Computing Machinery)
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)

questions.explanationMd: TREC was established by NIST to support shared IR evaluation benchmarks.

questions.questionMd: A medical literature search system is designed to ensure clinicians find every relevant study on a drug interaction. Which evaluation metric is most appropriate?

options.text: P@5, because clinicians typically only read the first five results returned
MAP, because it rewards retrieving all relevant documents and penalises any that are missed
MRR, because clinicians only need to find the single most authoritative study for each query
NDCG@10, because graded relevance most accurately reflects a clinician's document preferences

questions.explanationMd: For comprehensive retrieval tasks, MAP rewards systems that retrieve relevant documents throughout the ranked list and penalizes misses.

questions.questionMd: In IR significance testing, bootstrap resampling estimates confidence intervals by which procedure?

options.text: Randomly splitting the document corpus into halves and comparing system scores on each half
Repeatedly sampling queries with replacement from the evaluation set and recomputing the metric each time
Shuffling relevance judgments across queries to simulate a null distribution
Running the retrieval system multiple times with different random seeds and averaging the results

questions.explanationMd: Bootstrap resampling draws query samples with replacement and recomputes the metric to estimate uncertainty.

questions.questionMd: In SPIMI, why is only the dictionary key set sorted once per block rather than sorting all `(term, doc_id)` pairs as BSBI does?

options.text: Sorting is deferred entirely to the final merge phase, which processes pairs from all blocks simultaneously
SPIMI uses integer term_ids that are already numerically sorted, eliminating the need to sort strings
Doc_ids are appended in document-processing order directly to each term's list
SPIMI processes each document twice: once to assign term_ids and once to sort the pairs

questions.explanationMd: SPIMI builds postings lists directly while scanning documents, so it only needs to sort the dictionary keys before writing a block.

questions.questionMd: In Boolean retrieval, an OR query between two terms produces results by applying which set operation to their postings lists?

options.text: Set difference — documents containing the first term but not the second
Set complement — all documents not containing either term
Set intersection — documents containing both terms simultaneously
Set union — documents containing either term or both

questions.explanationMd: Boolean OR corresponds to the union of postings lists.

questions.questionMd: For which type of query is Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) the most appropriate evaluation metric?

options.text: E-discovery tasks where both high precision and high recall are legally required
Ad-hoc multi-document queries evaluated over a large corpus with hundreds of relevant documents
Navigational or single-answer queries where users care only about finding the first correct result
Medical literature searches requiring comprehensive coverage of all relevant studies

questions.explanationMd: MRR focuses on the rank of the first relevant result, so it is best for navigational or single-answer tasks.

questions.questionMd: A system has a high Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR). What does this indicate about its retrieval behavior?

options.text: The system retrieves all relevant documents within the top 10 results
The system maintains good Precision across a wide range of Recall levels simultaneously
The system's ranked list is longer than competitors, covering more of the corpus
The system has a very high Precision@1 but low Recall across all cutoffs

questions.explanationMd: High AUC-PR indicates strong precision is maintained as recall increases across many thresholds.

questions.questionMd: In the Average Precision formula `AP = (1/R) × Σ P@k`, what does the summation run over?

options.text: All rank positions from 1 to the total number of retrieved documents
Only the rank positions `k` where the retrieved document is relevant
The top-k positions specified by the evaluation cutoff
All positions where the retrieved document is irrelevant, as a penalty term

questions.explanationMd: AP sums precision only at ranks where a relevant document is retrieved, then divides by the total number of relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: Three queries yield Average Precision scores of 0.72, 0.45, and 0.38 for a system. What is the MAP?

options.text: 0.550, computed as the median of the three AP values
0.720, because MAP reports the highest AP score across all queries
1.550, because MAP sums the AP values without dividing by the number of queries

questions.explanationMd: MAP is the mean of AP values: `(0.72 + 0.45 + 0.38) / 3 = 0.5167`, approximately 0.517.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, what does the scheme `lnc` specify for document weighting?

options.text: Logarithmic TF, no IDF, cosine normalization
Natural TF, no IDF, cosine normalization
Log-average TF, natural IDF, no normalization
Logarithmic TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: `lnc` expands to logarithmic TF (`l`), no IDF (`n`), and cosine normalization (`c`).

questions.questionMd: What is the primary reason that lemmatization requires Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging to work correctly?

options.text: POS tagging is needed to filter out stopwords before lemmatization begins
Without POS tagging, lemmatization cannot distinguish between nouns and proper nouns
The same word form can have different base forms depending on its grammatical role
Lemmatization uses a dictionary that is indexed by POS tag rather than by word form

questions.explanationMd: A word's lemma can depend on whether it is used as a noun, verb, adjective, or another grammatical category.
